DOMINION-PROVINCIAL CONFERENCE ISSUES TO BE FACED AT FEBRUARY MEETING-TABLING OF FEDERAL PAPERS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, all hon. members know that a second meeting of the federal-provincial constitutional conference will take place next week in Ottawa.
At the first meeting, which was held in February last year, the heads of 11 governments participating in the conference agreed that the revision of the constitution they had undertaken was so important that it had to be attended to on a permanent basis until completion.
Unanimously, the Premiers recognized that, in view of the urgency of the task, the conference should not be adjourned but rather suspended to be resumed periodically. They also agreed that such an important task required the creation of a standing committee of officials who would be entrusted with the heavy responsibility of making investigations and reporting.
Moreover, they agreed that the scope of the undertaking entailed the establishment of a secretariat.

In February of 1968 there was unanimity in recognizing the perils that were besetting confederation, and in the importance of identifying and offsetting those perils by constitutional means. I have no hesitation in saying, Mr. Speaker, that the importance of this task of constitutional review has not lessened in the past 12 months. Nor do I hesitate to say that in my belief the task is even more urgent now than it was when we began a year ago. It would be folly of the most dangerous sort for us in 1969 to persuade ourselves that the discontent in French Canada which we all recognized in 1968-and the causes of which the first session of the conference dedicated
itself to removing-has in any appreciable measure disappeared. It would be hypocritical of us as legislators if we assumed, in the face of the steadily mounting evidence to the contrary in our society, that the individual human being needs no protection of his basic rights against the inroads of governments and the bureaucratic institutions and agencies which governments spawn. It would be an act of irresponsibility if we accepted the simplistic argument that there is nothing wrong with Canada that a revision of revenue sharing would not correct.
[DOT] (2:10 p.m.)
Prime Minister Pearson stated last February that at stake in this sweeping process of constitutional review and reform was nothing less than Canada's survival. I would not be candid if I did not say that today, one year later, the stake has not in my opinion changed. Canada's survival remains in issue.
If we are not able to take whatever steps are necessary to provide in this country equality of opportunity to all Canadians- equality which reveals no exceptions based on use of either of the official languages, or on regional economic disparities, or on basic individual freedoms-then we shall have failed. We shall have disappointed the expectations of the Fathers of Confederation. And we shall have disappointed as well the expectations of persons in many other countries who regard Canada as an example of a workable federal system in a co-operating bilingual community.
I believe that we shall not fail. I believe that we are capable of meeting successfully the challenge that faces us, which is no less than a systematic and comprehensive review of the structural framework of our Canadian society.

Such a review involves the establishment of priorities, as well as a selection of means which are necessary, according to the Canadian government, to carry them out. That is the subject of the document "The Constitution and the People of Canada" which sets forth the position of the federal government.
Mr. Speaker, I would now like to table English and French copies of this document.
February 6, 1969

Tabling of Government Papers [English]

speakeroldname: Hon. Robert L. Stanfield (Leader of the Opposition):
subtopic: DOMINION-PROVINCIAL CONFERENCE ISSUES TO BE FACED AT FEBRUARY MEETING-TABLING OF FEDERAL PAPERS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I hope I create no security problems for the Prime Minister by thanking him in public for his courtesy in providing me with an advance copy of the document he has just tabled. I appreciate his courtesy.
As the Prime Minister indicated, the document relates to the constitution, as some of us thought it might, and not to fiscal problems or problems of economic disparity which exist with the present constitutional arrangements. Although this booklet envisages a comprehensive review of constitutional problems, the proposals contained in it relate to a limited number of areas. There is a preamble which states purposes. The proposals of the booklet relate also to human rights, Senate reform and Supreme Court reform. Yet there is no specific proposal relating to the division of powers within the country. I presume that while the federal government is prepared to hear discussions on the subject, it is not making any proposals in this regard. Also, no specific proposal is made about any amending formula. The booklet is extensive in scope but nevertheless covers only a fraction of the constitutional problems and questions facing the country. Many of its statements seem to flow from previous statements of positions. There are some statements in it regarding provincial constitutions. The wisdom of putting into writing some of our unwritten conventions is questioned. We must be cautious in approaching this matter.
Perhaps the newest suggestions relate to the Senate and the Supreme Court. These suggestions are most interesting and I expect hon. members of the house and the people of the country will wish to study them carefully.
I do not rise at this time, Mr. Speaker, to emphasize any objections I might have to the proposals before us, or to express any differences of opinion. The document sets forth some limited objectives, and I must make it clear that I join with the Prime Minister in emphasizing the importance of the questions raised in it. It is important that we should succeed in having a constructive conference, one which will enable us to make progress toward strengthening the country. This is a subject of worry and concern, particularly in view of the seemingly small area in which agreement Was reached by the officials of the various governments, as disclosed by documents summarizing the conference they held.

So it would be difficult to exaggerate the importance of the outcome of the constitutional conference. I do not expect, and I do not think the people of Canada expect solutions to all our difficulties; but we hope and pray for progress.
As I said, Mr. Speaker, I did not rise to criticize or to express any reservations I might have or any differences of opinion that might exist with regard to priorities to be followed. Regardless of whatever difference of opinion there may be concerning these proposals, its great underlying purpose is to strengthen the country. I accept the conference on that basis; we all fervently hope this will be the consequence of its deliberations. I and my colleagues in this party extend our good wishes to the Prime Minister and his associates, as well as to the premiers of the provinces. We hope the conference will be noteworthy for its wisdom, moderation and understanding, indeed for the patriotism of those who participate.
I wish to make a statement which might possibly be misunderstood as implying criticism, but I put it forward after much consideration as a constructive argument. There is a reference in the document tabled by the Prime Minister to the importance of improving the spirit of co-operation between the federal government and the provinces with a view to reaching a genuine solution rather than suffering more from some of the difficulties which have occurred through the years. There is a grave uneasiness, Mr. Speaker, among the provinces regarding the willingness of the federal government to co-operate in solving fiscal and economic problems faced by the provinces.
The Prime Minister has emphasized this will be a constitutional conference, that fiscal and economic matters will be discussed in the constitutional aspects, but not with regard to their workings under the constitution as it exists. If this is the position, then I suggest it is of the utmost importance that the government give firm assurance to the provinces before the conference begins that it is prepared to co-operate fully in trying to reach solutions to problems which exist. The federal government should not merely give an assurance that it is prepared to confer fully and without restriction on these matters at an early date; it must consider taking some definite steps which would generate trust. There should be concrete terms and a genuine desire to consult and co-operate.
This government has proposed two tax measures which have not yet been adopted.
February 6, 1969	COMMONS
One of these is the estates and gifts tax, which is not a revenue item but is proposed as a measure of reform. This measure is resented by quite a number of provinces because of the lack of consultation, and one can make a good case in suggesting that the provinces ought to have been consulted with regard to this matter. I suggest it would be a concrete indication of the government's desire to cooperate, and might very well substantially improve the circumstances in which the conference meets, if the government were to say they would defer further consideration of this bill until there has been an opportunity for full consultation with the provinces.
I would also suggest that the government give further consideration to permitting the provinces to share in the so-called 2 per cent development tax. This is another source of real irritation. This is another way in which the government could take a concrete step which would give real and convincing evidence of its desire to co-operate in matters which strictly may not be before this conference, and yet may well have a very profound effect upon its success.
[DOT] <2:20 p.m.)
I do not put these suggestions forward lightly, Mr. Speaker. I realize that many of the suggestions which I am putting forward involve problems for the federal government, but I do emphasize the immense importance of the success of this conference upon the constitution. I do emphasize the need of the government of Canada to take every reasonable concrete step within its ability to create a belief among the provinces in the desire of the federal government to participate in creating a sense of confidence. I suggest that this is a wise course, and the government should not risk any failure in confidence resulting from a failure to take one or two steps I have suggested.

Mr. Speaker, I also want to thank the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) for letting me have a copy of this document, as he did other leaders of other parties in the house. Of course, Mr. Speaker, it goes without saying that I wish him and his colleagues and the spokesmen for the provinces the very greatest possible success, in view of the importance of the conference, but I must say that I have some profound doubts about the approach which is revealed in the document the Prime Minister has tabled today.

Tabling of Government Papers
First it must be noted-and the Prime Minister really recognized this-that it is a sad and disturbing fact that the constitutional conference which opens next Monday will open in a much less hopeful atmosphere than was the case a year ago. It also seems to me, and I am sorry to be driven to this conclusion, that the paper tabled by the Prime Minister, and his comments today, may not help to move the conference forward in a dynamic and fruitful direction.
The responsibility for this worsening situation is probably shared by all governments to some extent, but in my opinion it lies primarily with the federal government for reasons which I will indicate. Mr. Speaker, the document tabled by the Prime Minister, which I have studied very carefully, in my opinion discloses a myopic view of the Canadian problem, and is again an example of the purely legalistic approach which the government takes on so many matters. To me the document discloses a complete disregard for the basic social and economic storms which daily grow in intensity in Canada.
If you look at the paper you will find it deals with the instruments of government, with the Governor General and the cabinet, the House of Commons and the Senate, the Supreme Court of Canada and related matters. It reiterates the federal government's desire for an entrenched Bill of Rights-to which I will come back in a moment-but neither the paper nor, on the whole, the Prime Minister's comments contains any reference of substance to the problems of taxation, of revenues, of economic planning and development, or of the division of powers and responsibilities for the two levels of government.
If I may put it this way, Mr. Speaker, it seems to me that the provincial leaders come to Ottawa next Monday for bread, and in the spirit of Marie Antoinette the federal government insists that they have cake. No one denies-and I make this comment because I share with others great anxiety about the conference and the future of our country-no one denies the importance of considering the ways in which the instruments of government in Canada must be brought up to date. But instruments of government can be fashioned sensibly only in relation to the functions which they are to perform, and one of the two most important facts facing Canada today is the disarray of our economic and social condition as between the federal government and the provincial governments. The other is the question of language rights.
February 6, 1969

Tabling of Government Papers
I suggest that the overwhelming majority of Canadian people are concerned with finding new and relevant ways of meeting pressing social and economic needs, rather than with the structures of institutions, important though they may be. What I wish to emphasize is that the concentration in the paper on the structural framework may meet with indignant resistance from many if not all provincial leaders, and in my opinion such resistance will be justified.
The time has come for placing at the head of the constitutional discussions the role of the spending power of the federal government, the ways in which all provinces can be assisted to meet their pressing obligations to the Canadians within their borders, and the ways in which we can establish a system of comprehensive planning and co-ordination by both levels of government-planning with regard to priorities, tax rates, tax-mix, budgetary changes and even monetary policy. Nor is it reasonable to expect that these subjects can be discussed on a purely theoretical level. The opportunity must be given at the conference next week for a discussion which is relevant to the immediate problems, as well as to future developments.
I suggest that if the Prime Minister continues to insist that the discussion next week must be confined within a legal constitutional framework, the meeting will come up against insuperable difficulties and the responsibility will be primarily his. In order to succeed the conference next week will require effective recognition and meaningful discussion of the basic social and economic problems which bedevil the rich provinces, and frustrate the poor ones.
In one other respect the atmosphere in Canada has suffered some deterioration. A year ago it looked as if the equality of the two official languages in Canada, was on the verge of becoming a fact, as if the fears and objections had been, if not removed at least allayed. This now appears to have been too rash a conclusion. Perhaps the deterioration started with the ill-advised, shortsighted and rather bigoted actions in a few places in the province of Quebec where the language rights of the English speaking minority were seriously challenged. This is a great pity.
I do not see any reason for this development. Every Canadian, who believes as I and many of us do in the value and richness of bilingualism in Canada as well its contribution to Canada's future unity, cannot but deeply regret this retrogression in that great

province. But deterioration is by no means limited to the province of Quebec. It is evident in some other provinces as well, and was climaxed by the declaration of the three prairie premiers a few days ago with respect to the official languages bill which is now before parliament. I hope with all my heart the premiers of the prairie provinces will be persuaded at the conference to change their position on this point. It will require an immense effort of patience and understanding, in order to regain the ground lost in this aspect of our Canadian life. One can only hope the effort will be made, not only by the Prime Minister and federal spokesmen but also by many of the provincial leaders, in order that it may succeed.
[DOT] (2:30 p.m.)
Finally, on previous occasions spokesmen for our party have made clear our support of the idea of an entrenched bill of rights, including linguistic rights. I want to assure the Prime Minister that our party is firm in its conviction that such a provision in our constitution would enhance liberty and freedom in our Canadian society and deserves the continuous support of all thinking Canadians.
We are engaged in an exercise of monumental importance for the future of the Canadian people. The demand and the need for re-assessing the functions of the two levels of government and for reconstituting the instruments which serve them are recognized by all.
A Prime Minister and a federal government which has a broad and deep vision of the social and economic framework and of the need for fundamental changes can give dynamic leadership to this search. On the other hand, a government which confines itself within arid areas of legalistic argument and a purely structural framework, as unhappily now appears to be the case, can unwittingly shortcircuit an urgent national undertaking. I say these words, critical though they are and are intended to be, because of my anxiety about the present climate and the atmosphere in which the conference will meet, and the arid legalism with which alone the document tabled is filled.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker,
I only had a few minutes before this sitting began to look over this document just handed to us by the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau). This paper should create an impact and serve
February 6, 1969

as a working instrument during the federal-provincial conference beginning next week.
Mr. Speaker, I think that the federal-provincial conference which took place last year was a preliminary step to the one commencing next week. As a matter of fact, it has been considered by several persons that the first conference cleared the way on the question of bilingualism. I am of the opinion that the results achieved by the conference beginning next Monday will be proportional to the good will of the premiers and officials participating in it.
Like most people, I have noticed that some of the provincial delegates will be attending this conference with the intention of discussing financial priorities rather than the program proposed this afternoon by the Prime Minister.
This attitude leads me to believe that, for the provinces as a whole, the primary objective would rather be one of economics than one of languages or constitution. Therefore, as the working instrument offered by the central government does not, if I am not mistaken, deal at all with monetary or economic objectives, some provinces will be disappointed in the orientation of the talks.
In my estimation, due to the prevailing attitude, the priority objective is indeed of a constitutional nature, that is constitutional reform. However, I would think that efficient measures should be taken in order to achieve the proposed objectives.
On the matter of Confederation, the government is putting forward four objectives. I would like at this time to quote the third one which is as follows:
To promote national economic, social and cultural development, and the general welfare and equality of opportunity for all Canadians in whatever region they may live, including the opportunity for gainful
work-
Mr. Speaker, not only do I think that this objective has not been reached in our 100 years of Confederation, I even believe that we are still very far away from it, since we have now much too many unemployed, much too many Canadians who do not have jobs, or do not enjoy the comfort they are entitled to. Governments who for the last 100 years have followed one another, just as the present government, have denied them that right, and today again, we are making the same proposal, we are trying to reach the same objectives.
What is the government offering by means of this amendment to the Constitution, by this

Tabling of Government Papers constitutional review? What is it offering in order to reach that objective? I have not seen anything in the document, Mr. Speaker, and if the representatives of the provinces are coming to the conference next week in this state of mind, they will be very disappointed indeed, because the government is not proposing anything to improve the present situation.
I think that this aspect of the constitutional reform was forgotten and that it should be added on the order paper. I hope that the provincial delegates who are crying the loudest for fiscal benefits will at least propose a reform of our monetary system to the federal government, so that it might become what it should be, not a source of revenue to refloat departmental budgets and defray the cost of government administration, but a source of revenue designed to take the money from where it is not needed, when there is a surplus. However, this is not the case right now.
The provincial premiers will be here next week and they will be fighting to find out which level of government will be the first to take from the peoples' pockets the money needed for administrative purposes.
According to me, this is not the purpose of taxation. The government had better offer sources of income to them, which would enable them to administer the provinces, and then establish a taxation system in order to secure surplus money where it can be found, and the provinces should put forward proposals in that connection, since the federal government does not do so.
However, I trust that next week the conference will give all Canadians a glimmer of hope that will enable them to look forward to the days when they will have an equal chance to live, wherever they might choose to settle.

speakerposition: Minister of Industry; Minister of Trade and Commerce

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I had very constructive meetings in Vancouver on Tuesday with all elements of the industry concerned with grain movements. Present at the meeting were officials of the Canadian Wheat Board, members of the grain transportation committee and the producers advisory committee to the Canadian Wheat Board.
With regard to the existing backlog in the grain movement to and from the west coast

February 6, 1969
Movement of Grain
ports, I wish to report that the Canadian National and Canadian Pacific railways have given me their firm assurances that the existing backlog, occasioned in particular by the recent severe weather, will be corrected promptly. The elevator companies have assured me that the proper grains, and grades of grain, will be loaded at country points, as has been the case in recent days, in accordance with Canadian Wheat Board instructions, and that box cars will be unloaded without delay at terminal positions.
In private meetings, I was pledged the capacity and the continued co-operation of labour in meeting the challenge of the coming weeks. Given these firm assurances, and with more normal temperatures expected, I am confident that the situation at Vancouver will be corrected promptly. It would be folly of course for me to give an exact date as to when normalcy will return.
The discussions I had in Vancouver were both frank and enlightening. While I do not wish to be specific at this stage, it was conceded during these meetings that mistakes had occurred in recent weeks-mistakes that were extremely difficult to correct rapidly because of the unusually severe weather in January. In order to obtain the full picture of what actually happened, I suggest that hon. members consider hearing representatives of the railways, the elevator companies and the Canadian Wheat Board before the agriculture committee later in March. I consider that, in the interest of the grain producers, the efforts of those responsible in the grain industry should at this stage be directed as a matter of the highest priority to moving grain.
With regard to the demands for a transport controller made by some opposition members, and by premiers of the western provinces as well as by some government supporters, it is the confirmed opinion of everyone concerned-the producer representatives, the Canadian Wheat Board, the elevator companies, the railways and the Board of Grain Commissioners-that the present two co-ordinating committees in Winnipeg and Vancouver are better able to cope with the present situation than would be a transport controller. I am in full agreement with this position.
The situation in Vancouver highlights the importance of the excellent work of the grain transportation committee in the past two and a half years. The committee has fully accepted that in the long run the use of unit trains, larger country elevators and computerized

control are essential. The desirable objective is to establish a more efficient grain handling system in the interest of reducing costs to farmers and maximizing export efficiency. The basic research has now been completed and a new shipping order system has been developed. Basically, this system will involve 50 shipping blocks instead of 2,000 individual shipping stations. The first two shipping blocks will go into operation on an experimental basis in February in the Medicine Hat area, and in the Dauphin area in March. If the system works satisfactorily in these two areas, then it will be expanded for the whole of western Canada.
[DOT] (2:40 p.m.)
This work must be given the highest priority in order to ensure that we are equipped to take care of unusual demand situations. Many representatives at the first meeting of the Canada Grains Council expressed support for the need to modernize our grain handling system.
Finally, Mr. Speaker, I shall be in close touch with the situation in order to ensure that progress is in conformity with the assurances I received in Vancouver.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, we on this side of the house commend the minister for going out to Vancouver, ascertaining the direct cause of the problem and doing whatever he thought would eliminate or alleviate the difficulties the farmers now have to face. We had hoped he would have made this trip at least a month ago or, in fact, two months ago, when we had the first indication that Japan was not satisfied with the grading quality of United States wheat. The warning signs were then issued that trouble would arise in Vancouver because of the congestion that could well develop with regard to the necessity of having dry and high grade wheat there, and also damp grain which had to be dried, which would perhaps result in a lower grade quality wheat being stored.
The minister in his statement suggested that on his trip to Vancouver he ascertained there was an existing backlog of grain. This is an important admission on behalf of the government. Up until now the government has tried to shrug this problem off by saying it was a situation that arose only because of extraordinarily bad weather conditions. The minister also said that mistakes had occurred in recent weeks. We are interested in this admission by the government.
February 6, 1969

The minister also suggested that the railroad companies had assured him that the difficulty could be resolved, and because of these assurances he felt that the mistakes made in respect of shipping conditions could promptly be corrected. He did not tell us what the causes were and how, all of a sudden, the railroads could assure him that they would improve the situation.
The minister's statement suggests that the railroads have been negligent in the movement of grain up until this time, but they are going to pull up their socks after having talked to him. He did not say this, but he suggested it in his statement. We in this house know the problem that is involved. If there were not enough diesel locomotives with which to move the grain, why did not the government obtain some on a rental basis from the United States?
The minister also suggested that a new shipping order would go into effect, after due consultation with all the people in the grain trade, in an effort to reduce the cost to the farmers. The farmers were not consulted. All the representatives of the grain trade were consulted, except the producers. The producers themselves should have been consulted in this regard. It is suggested that the new shipping order will involve 50 shipping blocks, rather than 2,000 individual shipping stations. The minister's words suggest to me-and we will later examine them closely-the initial breakdown of the quota system, which ensures fair and equal opportunity for all farmers, if the system is properly administered, to deliver their grain.
The minister suggested, also, that the interested parties could be called before the agriculture committee. We commend this suggestion. I am sure the agriculture committee will want to know whether the railroads have been at fault, and why the trouble developed. It will want to know why, if the Wheat Board was at fault, the situation was allowed to develop. The committee will want to know what was the breakdown of communications which created this backlog of grain. We will want to know how the costs to the producer are to be reduced. If 50 shipping blocks are provided, this will in effect make the farmer deliver his grain to a shipping point that is perhaps much farther from the point to which he now has to deliver. This will increase the farmer's cost.
We on this side of the house are concerned about these questions. Surely the farmers should have been consulted before action was
Movement of Grain
taken. The farm unions, the Canadian Federation of Agriculture, and representatives of the producers should have been consulted about whether a transport controller was really necessary. The minister in his statement said that the situation in Vancouver highlighted the importance of the excellent work of the grains transportation committee, which has been in effect for the past two and a half years. Surely if the grains transportation committee is the solution, with one committee in Winnipeg and one in Vancouver, and the minister saw evidence of excellent work there, there should not have been this backlog. If the minister is right, why has there been this ball-up of grain movement? We on this side of the house are not convinced that a transport controller, with absolute authority for the movement of grain, could not play an effective role in clearing as quickly as possible the backlog of grain that exists and the problems we have at Vancouver.
We are very, very disappointed that the minister did not mention anything about the government picking up the demurrage charges for the grain now at Vancouver. The demurrage charges for the ships waiting there should be picked up by the federal government. The minister said this problem arose because of weather conditions. If it did arise because of weather conditions, surely it was an act of God and the government should help the farmers by at least paying the demurrage charges of the ships at Vancouver. The government should at least pay these charges for the first three months of this year. Surely this is not asking too much of the government. If the government wants hon. members on this side of the house to sincerely believe it is interested in helping the producers, it should do something to alleviate the problem in this regard rather than helping the middleman, because by its action the government is just increasing the problems of the producers.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, it is a good thing the minister finally went west, and saw for himself the situation that we face. I am sorry he has not seen fit to appoint a transport controller, or better still a co-ordinator who will take into consideration the whole movement of grain from the prairies to the west coast. The minister is, in effect, asking us to accept the proposition that the very committees which have failed to deal effectively with the situation in the immediate past are to be depended upon to do so in the

February 6, 1969
Movement of Grain
immediate future. We are supposed to depend on them to deliver the goods.
Essentially, we are still in the "wait and see" situation which we have experienced since last fall in regard to this problem. We will probably have to "wait and see" for some time yet before we know whether this committee is doing effectively the job it is supposed to do. Our figures show there is less Wheat in store on the west coast than there was on January 24. Some 9,300,000 bushels are in store now as compared with about 12 million bushels then. In effect we have failed to keep supplies moving in fast enough to keep pace with the outward movement, let alone build up a reserve of grain so as to take care of sales as they are offered.
[DOT] (2:50 p.m.)
Farmers have a right to expect better cooperation from the grain handling companies and from the railways than they have received. We are asked to run our farms efficiently; this is constantly being preached to us. But our being efficient is not much use if services essential to moving the grain break down. We do not ask these companies to serve the industry out of a spirit of charity, or just to be good to us. They make money out of it, just as the farmers hope to do. But in a period of extreme need they have failed to deliver the goods. We all know this is a time of fierce competition for grain sales on the world market, and that this situation is likely to continue.
I am all in favour of the research which is presently being done to discover new systems of moving grain. If the grain companies and the railway companies can work out new methods in co-operation with the Department of Trade and Commerce, more power to them. But I am not satisfied that, up to now, they have made an all-out effort to get the grain in position.
I am pleased to have the assurance of the minister that steps will now be taken to this end. I hope those responsible for moving the grain do not let him down because, if they do, they are letting the farmers down also. What is badly needed is some confidence on the part of the farmer that this job is being properly handled. I will tell the minister through you, Mr. Speaker, that the confidence of the farmers in the government, the grain handling companies and in the railways is at an all-time low. If the people who purchase

our grain overseas come to the conclusion that we cannot be relied on to deliver it, we are in bad shape.
I shall be pleased to see representatives of the Canadian Wheat Board and of the grain handling companies appear before the Standing Committee on Agriculture. In fact, I asked that the representatives of the Wheat Board should appear before now, but I was told-and I accepted the statement at the time-that they were too busy to do so. I hope they were too busy. Let us not forget that the first order for wheat for Japan was given away back in November.
In closing I urge that steps be taken to keep a day to day tab on shipping orders out of the elevators, and that a similar day to day check be kept of car loadings and their movement. Remember, it is necessary to unload between 550 and 600 cars a day at the terminals in Vancouver if we are to keep up to our commitments. I see the minister agrees with me.

Mr. Speaker, I admit that the first time this serious question was raised in the house, I found it very difficult to determine who was right, since there were so many different opinions. Today, in the light of the minister's statement, I am sure that a problem existed. However, if one cares to set to work and to devote all one's energies to the task, it is possible to find a solution.
I congratulate the minister for his statement following his trip to western Canada to meet all the organizations interested in the movement of grain to various parts of Canada and also abroad.
Having listened to the encouraging remarks of the Minister of Industry, Trade and Commerce (Mr. Pepin), it will be interesting to follow the developments in this matter. I sun sure that all members will be much interested in following progress in the next few days, and that grain handling will be done normally, bringing relief not only to the government, but also to grain producers who had to face a very serious problem.
Therefore, I congratulate the minister and I can assure him that the members of the Ral-liement Creditiste will always be ready to help find a solution to problems which come under his department.

speechtext:
I should like to ask the Prime Minister whether he would consider a suggestion I made a little earlier about the government deferring further action on the bill relating to estate tax and income tax until the provinces have been conferred with and consulted. In view of the importance of the matter, would he give it immediate attention?
I should like to ask the right hon. gentleman also whether he would consider consulting with the premiers about the modification of the position the government has taken with regard to the so-called 2 per cent social development tax and the refusal of the government to share this tax revenue with the provinces.

subtopic: DOMINION-PROVINCIAL CONFERENCE CONSULTATION WITH PROVINCES BEFORE PROCEEDING FURTHER WITH TAXING MEASURE
speechtext:
As to the first suggestion, my comment is, of course, that this proposal was made in the 29180-330
Inquiries of the Ministry budget by the Xvlinister of Finance last October and that he subsequently invited the provinces to discuss it with him. They have had several months in which to do so, and discussions have taken place. As the house knows, the Minister of Finance modified the proposals slightly in the light of those discussions. We felt this was sufficient consultation. Moreover, we repeat that we intend, when we overhaul in a basic way the tax system of this country, to proceed in the same way or alternatively by submitting a white paper. At that time the provinces will have even more time and more specific invitations to submit their views.
On the second point, about giving the provinces part of the 2 per cent tax, or the totality of the tax as some provinces suggest, my only comment is that if there were agreement by the Leader of the Opposition to the effect that he would not mind if we did not balance our budget, or if he recommended we come out with some other tax of our own for the purpose of balancing the budget, then we might be prepared to consider this. We raise money because we need it; we raise money because we believe that the budget should be balanced; and we raise money because we want to use it for federal purposes. We believe that the country has to have the assurance that the federal government is aiming toward a balanced budget, which it would not be doing if it gave the money produced by its taxes to the provinces.

subtopic: DOMINION-PROVINCIAL CONFERENCE CONSULTATION WITH PROVINCES BEFORE PROCEEDING FURTHER WITH TAXING MEASURE

subtopic: DOMINION-PROVINCIAL CONFERENCE CONSULTATION WITH PROVINCES BEFORE PROCEEDING FURTHER WITH TAXING MEASURE

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker I think the government would be prepared, if the leaders of the various parties agree, to set some time aside in the house, as we offered at the time of the last federal-provincial conference, to debate the results of the conference or the substance of the paper.
On the establishment of a continuing committee to take up the constitutional problem, I do not believe that this government's position has changed from that of Mr. Pearson's government. We still think that such a committee would cause a great deal of delay in the constitutional process. It is already a fairly lengthy and difficult process, with representatives of ten provinces carrying on discussions with representatives of the federal government at the subcommittee level, at the committee level and then at the ministerial level. If all of this would then have to be processed as well through a house committee, especially a committee of the house whose membership might include opposition members who do not agree on what kind of constitution we need, I think an endless amount of time would be taken. I am hoping we will be able to proceed in a more urgent fashion.
However, this does not preclude a clear statement by opposition parties on what they think we should do with the monarchy, or what they think we should do with the executive function, whether we should keep our parliamentary democracy or adopt a congressional system, and so on. All of these views would be extremely helpful, but we think

speechtext: The house resumed, from Wednesday, February 5, consideration of the motion of Mr. Benson for the second reading and reference to a Committee of the Whole of Bill C-165, to amend the Income Tax Act and the Estate Tax Act, and the amendment thereto of Mr. Saltsman (p. 5191).

subtopic: INCOME TAX ACT AND ESTATE TAX ACT
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I choose to rise in support of this new estate tax legislation because along with my colleagues I have studied its features and consider it not only very good legislation but legislation which reflects the Liberal position in relation to taxation. In doing so it highlights the principal differences between the various political philosophies represented in this house.

subtopic: INCOME TAX ACT AND ESTATE TAX ACT
speechtext: A big "L"?

subtopic: INCOME TAX ACT AND ESTATE TAX ACT
speechtext:
A big "L" which has a small "1" connotation. It is legislation that is a distinct departure and, I believe, an improvement over that which previously existed. The recognition of the equal yet very special status of the widow is important. It recognizes the changing role of women in our society and their fundamental rights. At the same time it recognizes that they are still women, and for that we are truly grateful.
Now for the first time widows will not be faced with agonizing decisions for which they are frequently unprepared or unequipped at a time when they are making, I believe, the most difficult adjustment of their lives.

The small farm or small business will almost always be exempt. Those not so small will pay some tax as before. In some cases they will pay a little less and in others a little more depending on the circumstances, but in no case will their situation be so drastically different that it will change the ultimate disposition of the estate.
The demise of the family farm is a matter of serious concern to society, to government and, of course, to the farmers themselves. I submit that this problem exists with or without estate taxes. The prime concern of the farmer, indeed of all businessmen-and the farmer today must operate as a businessman-is that of economics, productivity and profitability. Another major factor in family farming is the willingness or lack of willingness of sons to remain on the farm. More and more farm children are choosing educational pursuits and skills which attract them to other endeavours and regions, particularly urban centres.
This legislation is being used as a smokescreen by some to place the blame for a much larger problem on the shoulders of the government. I hope it might have some beneficial results. Just as the farmer has had to change from the horse to the tractor, just as he has had to become more scientific in his approach to basic farming, the farmer now will have to be more inclined to seek needed professional advice in preparing his estate. He should consult a lawyer, accountant, trust company or even a well qualified life insurance underwriter to determine the structure of his assets in his lifetime and in preparation for his death.
The mortality rate among farmers is the same as for all Canadians, 100 per cent. I think the farmer or small businessman who seeks such advice will be surprised to learn how little, if at all, the new amendments affect him. If they do he has the pay-out period of five years now so that he can plan his pay-back of estate taxes if they are burdensome. Under a special appeal to the minister I am sure that in special circumstances he could have an even longer period.
In so far as penalizing success is concerned I suggest that this reflects a type of thinking that went out the window generations ago. Most of us in our society recognize that those who for a number of reasons are blessed with material success above the norm have an obligation to those less fortunate. Most men of wealth accept also the responsibilities of wealth; if they do not, they should.

Income Tax Act and Estate Tax Act
If these amendments meant that all wealth-was to be completely equalized and if they did not allow for reasonable retention of the main fruits of one's efforts, initiative and entrepreneurship, they would indeed warrant'-some of the hysterical criticism that the social and economic Neanderthals are hurling, but I suggest there is still a great deal left. I am not at all convinced that substantial inherited wealth is at all desirable for the proper development of one's children. We want to give these children a good start in life, a good education and an opportunity to prosper, but I do not think we necessarily want to give them a future on a silver platter. A sense of values comes into play here. Children today are questioning these values. I suggest to the gentlemen opposite and to my left that their value judgments, if indeed they are judgments at all rather than reflex actions, are far out of tune with our times and with the very children for whom they allege they speak.
This past weekend I had a constituent call me who was very concerned about this bill because he thought his estate was being absolutely devastated. In speaking to the man a little further and finally realizing who he was I found out that his estate consisted of many millions of dollars. The problem was whether he was going to leave $4 million or $5 million, $3 million or $5 million-it really does not matter very much. That man was very concerned about giving his children a good start. I suggest that children with $2 million or $3 million are not getting a bad start. On the other hand, there is the converse; I am not really sure this is a good start for kids.
There is an exception which should interest us as legislators. There is a very interesting tradition of inherited wealth being beneficial. This is in a case where families-the Ken-nedys perhaps are the best example-have gone into public service and have used that wealth constructively, even ill-gotten wealth, I think, in some cases. I should not mention names of families because some people might think I am singling out the Kennedys or the Rockefellers. But the result of the efforts of these families has been really quite valuable. It is families of this type we should choose to emulate among those who are fortunate enough to inherit such wealth.
There is another important economic factor involved. I refer to the continuation of the family business with family management. In my experience, for every example of successful second or third generation family management of a business there are at least ten
February 6, 1969
5224	COMMONS
Income Tax Act and Estate Tax Act examples of failure. Professional management is becoming more essential and this nostalgia for the good old days perpetrates a myth from which, if continued, the industries of this nation could suffer severely.
I do not believe the new estate taxes in themselves will result in additional sales of family businesses. I hope that such businesses will continue to be sold when the next generation does not have the drive, the desire or the skill to ensure their dynamic continuance. There are lots of Canadian dollars looking for investment as indicated in the York University study, but even foreign dollars combined with dynamic management are far preferable to home-grown and inherited mediocrity.
The pay-out period gives opportunity to dispose of the inheritance on a fair basis and make the proper deal that should be made. It will not involve a forced sale because there are many people looking for businesses today.
Then we have this talk about killing initiative. The people who are supposedly affected by the highest rates are generally beyond the stage where money is the sole object. The money, the profitable balance sheet, is the scoreboard of success. These men want the challenge, the accomplishment, even the power, power to be used responsibly, I believe, and for constructive purposes. The men with ideas, the leaders, the entrepreneurs, the men who provide the dynamics of our society and economy have many motivations. Money is only one. After a certain level of accomplishment its value is used only as a measuring stick of success or for achieving greater success. Someone has said that most men are self-made but that only the successful admit it. I am not sure that is always true.

My friends in the N.D.P., I regret, fail to recognize the value of this device and the need for a realistic measurement of accomplishment. They somehow consider profit immoral while the greater immorality is the lack of profit, for it is profit that makes investment possible. It is profit that makes higher wages possible. It is profit that makes research possible, and it is profit that makes taxes possible. It is the misuse of profit or its achievement by improper means which is truly immoral. This immorality is almost as great as the toleration and encouragement of this immorality by others, including government.
This is a most interesting debate because the problems we are talking about are problems of success and of affluence. We have


people now with sufficient assets to be concerned about estates, although we find a lot of their concerns are unfounded. How much more fortunate we are to face these problems than problems of the lack of prosperity. Certainly there are areas and pockets which have been shamefully neglected and with which we should be dealing much more vigourously, but in the main we are all living better than ever before.
Our problems are problems of priority in necessities which we considered luxuries a few years ago. Most people today do not face the difficult decision of whether to buy a car but really how expensive a car and, in a growing number of cases, how many cars. Many people are worried about whether to buy a coloured television set or a second black and white set for the recreation room or the bedroom, or a new outboard motor or a skidoo. This does not apply to all our population but to a very large and growing segment of it.
We have so much going for us in this country that we should really be counting our blessings. Certainly we have problems that we must face and tackle vigourously. Some of these will be solved and others will not, and when we solve some then there will be new ones we never expected. The danger is in losing perspective. Some cry gloom and doom whenever we make a progressive step, as we are now in updating and humanizing our estate laws, changes I support with considerable enthusiasm, and it worries me terribly that there is an element of a lunatic fringe which brands it socialist or neo-communistic. Some of my friends opposite are encouraging this hysteria. I am afraid they are backing themselves into a corner from which they may never emerge, but perhaps that is a good thing.
We must have a responsible alternative to the government, but by encouraging this hysteria and this lunatic fringe hon. members do not prove themselves to be a responsible alternative. Instead, they run the risk of losing their credibility. I think this is a pity because one never knows but that in 15 or 20 years the people of Canada might want a change of government. Those who seek to fill the position at that time may well have lost this responsibility. I do not suggest they have done so; I just suggest it is possible.

Opposition): Mr. Speaker, it has been made pretty clear by the Minister of Finance (Mr. Benson) that we are not dealing here with a

The minister told us yesterday that only 5 per cent of the people of Canada would ever pay estate taxes. I do not know whether he intended to suggest that what happens to the other 95 per cent is of little concern-I do not suppose he really meant that-but that was one possible inference to be taken from his attitude.
When the minister put forward his bill in its initial form, which would have meant taxing very small estates, he must have known that it would have affected hundreds of thousands of estates. The minister shakes his head, but considering an estate of $20,000 to $40,000 and the constant deterioration of the value of money, it would have begun to affect a very substantial proportion of the Canadian people.

speechtext: A good question.

subtopic: INCOME TAX ACT AND ESTATE TAX ACT

Well, reform means change. But it seems to me that the opposition-and I am not speaking now only about hon. members opposite but also of opposition on this side of the house-tends to say: we want the reforms but don't change this, or don't change that. How can there be reform without change? This is the issue which is involved in the bill before us.
I agree with the Leader of the Opposition that this measure should possibly have been introduced along with other reform measures. I believe Carter was right when he said that if it was intended to introduce a large number of changes, especially in the taxation field, they should all be introduced together, not piece by piece. You see, Mr. Speaker, the people who will be hurt by this bill are not likely to forget it when we introduce another measure later which will be of benefit to them, for example, the single taxation of corporations. On the other hand, members on the other side who are pleased to see the introduction of this bill will condemn us anyway if we remove the burden of double taxation from corporations. All these changes should have been introduced together. Possibly the Leader of the Opposition was right on this point.
However, there is another point to be considered. It is essential that as much time as possible be given to those who are responsible for the planning of estates. The disposal of estates has to be thought out carefully and in advance. Wills have to be made. Notice is now given that when this bill becomes law all those responsible for estates must prepare themselves.
Let me deal with some of the objections raised specifically by the hon. member for Edmonton West. He criticized the bill because it would mean, he said, the dispersion of capital. This argument was based on the presumption that all inherited wealth is immediately invested in corporate or other fields of investment. This is nonsense. Inherited
February 6, 1969

wealth is not, in the main, the source of investment capital. I should like to know where the hon. member got the facts upon which he based his presumption. I do not think that presumption is valid. Nor, as the hon. member for York North (Mr. Danson) pointed out a little while ago, is the presumption valid that there is something sacred or sanctified about the continuation of family corporations. I think he was accurate when he said that approximately 10 per cent of such corporations are successful and the majority not. It is not likely that we will get succession of ability merely because a son's father had brain and drive. This is not so.
[DOT] (4:20 p.m.)
Consider also that when most corporations reach the stage where succession duties become a problem a move is made toward public subscription, at the same time maintaining the power structure within the family unit or among friends. If there is any one thing in Canada that is the cause of inefficiency so far as industrial growth is concerned, it is that we tend too much to keep control of corporations in the hands of family units.
Mr. Porter, in his volume "The Vertical Mosaic", was quite right when he said that it is one of the detriments of Canadian corporate society that about 85 per cent of our wealth is controlled by 190 families. You cannot expect the constant and certain succession of ability merely because the father of the family left sons behind him to run the business. History and experience teach that the opposite is true. Facts from across the border indicate that it is much more advantageous to introduce new blood into a corporation than to keep it in the family. However, I accept the fact that the hon. gentleman was obviously quite successful in the business in which he engaged before becoming Leader of the Opposition and premier of Nova Scotia.
Let me say a word about farms. The hon. member for Edmonton West (Mr. Lambert) said that in cases where farmers have two or three sons working on the farm to make the enterprise successful who do not have any income of their own, it would be unfair when the father died to expect them to pay succession duties or estate tax. Let me put the proposition another way. What would the hon. gentleman say if I had stated that it would be quite proper, using the same analogy, to allow an executive in a plant to draw an income of, say, $4,000 a year and to receive $200,000 or $300,000 worth of corporation shares tax free when he retired? He
Income Tax Act and Estate Tax Act would scream blue murder. But the fact is that even though farmers' sons do not draw any income or pay income tax, they are still taxed at the death of their father.
As I have suggested to the minister, I would be in favour of letting beneficiaries amortize their inheritance, if they so chose, over a period of ten years by paying income tax annually and then having a lump sum tax free. But they cannot have it both ways. You cannot put one group of people into one category and, as the minister said, put another group in another category.
Further, the hon. gentleman said that there was something very evil about corporation farms rather than the preservation of family farms. It seems to me there is a place fox-family farms if people want to continue farming. But many western farmers are not really family farmers as much as men running a business. They have to watch the stock market and feed prices in the same way that other businesses have to watch for certain indicators. Provision should be made in other legislation to give them the same opportunity to receive capital and an adequate supply of labour. But the small family farmer is not going to be hit by this bill. He will not have an estate to worry about. It is the large farmer who runs a big farm as a business who will have to worry, the same as other large businesses; they are both in the same position. I can see no rationalization whatever in putting farmers in a position different from other citizens.
The corporate farm, which was condemned, is not in issue here. However, I submit that in some cases it can be justified. After all, if we are going to consider farming as an industry we have to make it as efficient as possible. If corporation fanning is the most efficient way for the industry to operate, then what is wrong with it? If the purpose were to have farms for the exclusive use of large corporations, that would be a different matter. But that is not the purpose. The purpose of farming is to produce the most on the least amount of land in the most efficient way.
Let me now get down to the main issue, which is whether we acknowledge the fact that there is such a thing as inherited privilege and whether we are going to perpetuate it in the face of world opinion and the movement forward. Everyone wants to leave a mark on this earth. It seems that Canadians and Americans especially want to leave something for future generations. But the fact is that future generations do not want it. They

If I read it correctly, it seems to me that we have said it is no longer important whether one parent has worked hard, whether he has saved money, whether he has the means to grant the privilege to his children of going to university, and another parent has not. What we have said is that we are going to put both in the same boat. If one student is a good student but does not have wealth behind him, he is put in the position where he can borrow money and also receive an education.
If hon. gentlemen opposite are insistent upon preserving inherited privilege, or if they question, as the Leader of the Opposition did, the rate of estate tax, which is really the same thing, then why should we not say that a man whose great grandfather made a great contribution politically should be entitled to certain privileges? Many Canadians were aware of the Prime Minister's thinking along socialist lines. Many were blinded by his supposed charisma but it did not fool the farmers of western Canada. They have mistrusted socialist ideas and that is why they did not send too many of his party to Ottawa. Certainly their mistrust of the Prime Minister was not misplaced, because his government in fact has introduced socialist legislation. Why will the burden be particularly great at this time? Looking at the agricultural industry we realize that slowly and surely the average age of today's farmer is becoming higher. The approximate age for farmers in Ontario is 60 years; Alberta, approximately 55; Saskatchewan, approximately 58. These farmers are at an age when they are concerned about having their sons or daughters inherit their farms.
Another reason it is too great a burden at this time is the accelerated inflation over the last ten years which has caused the price of farm land and machinery to increase vastly. The government and the Farm Credit Corporation are aware of this. The government set up an inquiry to see whether the prices of farm machinery could be lowered or, if not, kept at the same level. Every year since 1963 there has been a price increase of 4.5 per cent. The government has promoted a sharply inflationary condition. In his speech to the 122nd annual meeting of Canadian life insurance companies, Mr. Graham Towers said he was fearful governments could no longer control their spending. [DOT] (5:00 p.m.)
He said: Mr. Speaker, I do not want to take up the time of the house at any great length on the matter referred to in notice of motion No. 19 which asks for an order for a copy of all letters, reports and so on, the details of which you have just read. I do, however, have a few points I should like to put forward. First, there is the failure of the government to table the papers referred to and the significance of that failure as it bears upon the rights of members of parliament in representing the people of Canada. Second, I wish to comment on the present situation in our official dealings in respect of reported sightings of u.f.o.'s or flying saucers.
At the outset may I say that in respect of u.f.o.'s I am an agnostic. I neither believe nor disbelieve; I just do not know. I have no special interest in the matter. Indeed, the first time I heard the term u.f.o. I thought it had to do with the United Farmers of Ontario. So I am by no means a flying saucer devotee.
My reason for bringing up the matter in the first place and later and in asking for the tabling of papers was simply to comply with a request from constituents who, as are many other Canadians, are much interested in what reportedly happened to Mr. Stephen Michalak in eastern Manitoba last May when he was prospecting near Falcon Lake. According to Mr. Michalak, who later published a pamphlet on his experience, about noon that day he saw two oval-shaped objects glowing an intense scarlet approach overhead. While one stopped in mid-air the other landed on a flat rock nearby. After a few moments its companion resumed flight and swiftly disappeared. Overcoming his shock Mr. Michalak approached the landed object. He described the appearance of it in detail. He later touched it and the touch burned his rubber glove.
February 6, 1969

Mr. Michalak states that the object tilted up and released a sharp beam of heat that scorched his chest. It continued upward and disappeared. Immediately after this Michalak states that he experienced severe headaches and nausea and with difficulty returned to his home in Winnipeg. He later lost weight and developed a rash and other symptoms which were never clearly diagnosed.
It was this reported happening and the interest by my constituents which prompted me to write the National Research Council section which receives or records such sightings. I asked for a report on it. I was told that R.C.M.P., R.C.A.F., Health and Welfare and Geological Survey of Canada reports have been received by the branch, and while these would be made available to me to read if I would go to that office the branch would not agree to table the material.
It seemed to me then and now that this material should be made available to all members of parliament in the usual way so that it could be studied by any interested member. With this in mind, in October, 1968, I asked for the production of papers. When this was refused and the data was not tabled in the house I took the step of transferring the matter for debate.
I believe that in the field of unidentified flying objects the Canadian government does not show enough serious concern. The position of the government agency is exemplified by a statement in a letter to me from the head of the upper atmosphere research section of the radio and electrical division, National Research Council of Canada on September 27, 1968, which reads as follows:
In March of this year the N.R.C. accepted the responsibility for filing and cataloguing all u.f.o. reports sent to the federal government. We keep these on the non-meteoritic sighting file which is maintained as an auxiliary file to the fireball report file. This office acts as a co-ordinating headquarters, etc... It should be understood that we do not actively solicit non-meteoritic sightings, nor do we in general carry out field work of such sightings unless they show a fairly definite promise of giving useful scientific information-
In other words, there is no real or active interest by this division in the very large and conceivably important area of u.f.o. information. This government agency is out of tune with the desire for more knowledge in this new field by a great many serious-minded North Americans. It is estimated that no less than five million Americans now claim they have seen u.f.o.'s, and the United States government recently received a detailed report by a special body which spent some years and
Motions for Papers
half a million dollars to investigate alleged sightings. The fact that the report was of the opinion, in brief, that there was nothing to the stories and reports of u.f.o. incidents immediately aroused criticism by a number of scientifically oriented groups who are or appear to be very well informed to the contrary.
At any rate, I believe that in Canada we should have a more tangible policy regarding u.f.o. investigations. I think the government should table all information available pro and con about these phenomena. I think we should also consider that our own little earth is now sending out flying objects, and if life exists on other planets the flying objects which the U.S.A. and the U.S.S.R. are sending into space may very well appear to that form of life to be unidentified flying objects.
In conclusion, Mr. Speaker, I find the following brief comments by some well informed people of interest: "The existence of these machines is evident and I have accepted them absolutely"-Air Chief Marshal Lord Dowding; "I believe extra-terrestrial intelligences are watching the earth and have been visiting us for millenia in their flying saucers"-Dr. Hermann Oberth, rocket scientist; "I believe in u.f.o.'s"-Knut Hammarskjold, Director General of Internal Air Transport Association; "the hypothesis that these u.f.o.'s are extra-terrestrial surveillance... I regard as most likely"-Dr. James McDonald, physicist; "at first, without any question at all, I thought it was stuff and nonsense, but not any more"-Dr. J. Allen Hynek, astrophysicist.
I have two points. I think the papers should be tabled so that we can all find out what they say, and I believe Canada through its agency in this field should take a more serious interest in establishing the facts.

create a dangerous precedent that would not contribute to the good administration of the country's business and such has been the policy of the present and preceding governments.

subtopic: INCOME TAX ACT AND ESTATE TAX ACT
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, at five o'clock I was dealing with the effects the estate tax will have on what is generally considered to be the family farm or what has now become established in many places in western Canada as a farm of an economical and efficient size.
The minister suggested this tax would be a special burden on the farmer. He justified

this by saying farmers have received subsidies from the federal government during the years they operated the farm and it was only fair that this advantage should be equalized with the burden carried by the wage earner by imposing this special tax upon farmers. This change will involve $45 million. The minister stated he was not trying to raise more money by this change, which someone called a philosophical change, but claimed it would apply more fairly to all segments of the industry. If this is true, Mr. Speaker, it is a shame this government feels the farmer must have this special burden placed on him, particularly in the light of the report last fall of the Economic Council of Canada. Their report painted a vivid picture of Canadian agriculture in dire need of more capital. This tax is a direct tax on capital, there is no question about that.
The minister has said the estate tax in the past has brought in $200 million. The proposed changes are an attempt to shift $45 million of that figure to people in different occupations. I would like to ask the minister if these proposed changes will result in a drop in income from $200 million to $190 million?
Is the raising of the exemption from $20,000 to $50,000 going to have any real effect on the income the government receives? Surely, his computers have worked out some estimates as to what change in dollar income this will bring about.
The Canadian Federation of Agriculture has suggested the exemption on a once in a lifetime gift of a farm from father to son be increased from $10,000 to $25,000. I have suggested this figure be raised from $10,000 to $30,000. This would not involve many dollars and would lessen the burden the minister has placed on farmers.
The report, "Transfer Taxes: Their Effect on Productivity and Control of our Economy" published for the Ontario Economic Council has some interesting facts with regard to transfer taxes on capital. I quote from page 9 of the report:
As the economies of large-scale farm operations become more prevalent, and the world demand for food accelerates, are the working capital requirements of our agricultural industry to be compounded by the imposition of substantial transfer taxes on our farms?
This is exactly what the minister is doing. The report also points out that Canada leads 13 countries in the free world in transfer tax on capital. One commodity Canada is short of
February 6, 19S9

is capital. The Minister of Finance (Mr. Benson) should realize that this country is basically an importer of capital and therefore we should not have the highest possible taxes on that capital. There is a table on page 11 of the report which vividly illustrates the percentage of revenue which the government receives from transfer taxes. The report also vividly points out there is a direct relationship to economic growth and tax on capital. One example in the report is West Germany. Over the past 20 years this country has had the quickest acceleration of economic growth and the lowest tax on capital, a direct relationship between tax on capital and economic growth of the country.
We in this country complain of foreign ownership and what steps the government could adopt to allow more Canadians to take part in the growth and ownership of this wonderful country of ours.
[DOT] (8:10 p.m.)
As the hon. member for Edmonton West (Mr. Lambert) pointed out this increase in estate tax will encourage Americans to buy land and businesses in Canada. I will read again from the article quoting the hon. member for Coast Chilcotin (Mr. St. Pierre):
I'm worried that the estate tax is going to accelerate the sale of these ranches to foreigners. People just won't have the money to pay the estate taxes.
In a young and vibrant country like this, with all our natural resources and potential, we are taxing capital; yet capital is one of the commodities which we import and for which we pay high prices, first in interest rate and secondly in the loss of Canadian ownership. Canadians all across the country want to own more of the land and participate in the growth of the country.
In today's economy, the farmer works longer hours and receives less pay per hour of labour than workers in any other industry. In days gone by it was often said that a farmer lived poor and died rich. With this increase in estate tax he will continue to live poor, and he will die poor.

That is a very commendable attitude on the part of the Minister of Finance in our time. The minister has failed in certain respects in this bill before us to introduce or maintain equality in the proposed rates of taxation. The minister must be well aware that if there was some consolidated opposition to the proposed changes in estate tax rates it was first of all because he lately proposed to reduce drastically certain exemptions. These reductions would have had the effect of making estates of a rather modest size subject to taxation. He has since conceded that it is necessary, perhaps as a result of representations or pressures, to exempt estates under $50,000 from taxation. Surely, there must be some way in which to avoid this glaring lack of proportionality or progressiveness. At the $1 million mark there is, as I have said, a substantial reduction in tax. Would it not have been better to increase the exemption to a basic $50,000 and then to leave the marginal rate of tax on estates over $1 million at 54 per cent as it was, rather than reduce the marginal rate at the top so that the same marginal rate is being applied to inheritors of estates of $300,000 as it is to $1 million estates? They are paying the same marginal rate as those who will inherit estates of $1 million or $2 million. I do not think this is a very equitable way to proceed with what is alleged to be estate tax reform.
I would like to put on the record some figures with regard to the effective rate of taxation on estates of various sizes. Let us compare the old estate tax rates with the new ones. The effective rate on a $55,000 estate, for example, will be 50 per cent under the new proposals. On a $60,000 estate, the effective rate will be 50 per cent. On an $80,000 estate, the effective rate will be 36 per cent. The effective rate decreases gradually. I think it is possible to generalize as follows: With respect to estates valued at less than $90,000 the effective rate according to the new proposals will be 10 to 15 per cent higher than under the existing estate tax system. Under the existing law a survivorship pension in the hands of a widow forms part of the taxable assets of her estate, or more particularly her husband's estate. The amount of $160,000 for a young family which the father has provided through life insurance and other means is not a large estate if the wife has to face the future alone. 'We will tax you because the more you save the more you have, and so the more we will take away from you.'

I have referred to estate planning. I should like to draw your attention, Mr. Speaker, to a number of provisions in the bill and to comment on their implications as I see them. The minister has said on a number of occasions that gifts up to $2,000 a year by each parent to each child are to be tax free. That is to say, if you have a normal family of a mother, father and children, $4,000 each year may be transferred to each child each year until the death of the first partner. After that, $2,000 a year may continue to be passed on tax free. I wish to make two points clear. First of all, over a ten year period this provides an opportunity for parents to pass to each child $40,000.

Secondly, the transfer does not have to be in cash. If a parent makes gifts exceeding $2,000 a year to a child that parent is liable to pay gift tax on the cumulative total of such taxable gifts which are over and above the basic minimum I have just referred to. Through estate planning, it is possible to split estates and to minimize the effects of gift tax liability. For example, if one looks at the schedule one will see that accumulated gifts of $200,000 would be taxable at $71,500 and at the marginal rate thereafter of 75 per cent. If the gifts were split, and made by husband and wife, that is if they each gave $100,000, the tax is $21,250 for each parent, for a total of $42,500, which is $30,000 less than the figure I mentioned previously. The marginal rate also is only 36 per cent, half the marginal rate on the unsplit $200,000 accumulated gift.
[DOT] (9:20 p.m.)
May I refer quickly to other opportunities allowing for the transfer of assets to those of younger generations. I have already referred to the exemptions for younger children and to the fact that for each child under 11 years old the exemption is now $35,000. I referred in my example to a family of four children under the age of 10. The total exemption for that family would be $160,000. Similarly, the exemption in respect of disabled children has been considerably increased. An adult child aged 41, for instance, who is dependent because of infirmity would qualify for an exemption of $40,000, and provision is made for exemptions to dependant adult children up to $80,000. Surely, this is a compassionate move. For adult children not so dependent, the exemption is $10,000. I have referred also to the provision for the payment of estate tax over a period of five years in six equal instalments. This will enable estate planners to use much more latitude when considering ways and means of financing the tax, because it will take the heat off the forced sale.
One further point on estate planning: It may be argued that only those who are wealthy can afford the kind of tax advice which will enable them to undertake estate planning. I would say that anyone who has an estate of $50,000, or is likely to have such an estate, is quite able to afford the kind of tax advice needed to minimize the effect of estate taxation. The fact is that anyone who has an estate worth more than $50,000 should seek
