In conclusion, I should like to refer to the terms of the amendment. We are asked to give consideration to a complete revision of the federal tax legislation with a view to making revisions in such legislation which would be progressive and equitable. It seems to me, Mr. Speaker, that in the three months since these proposals were put forward in the budget resolutions there has been ample opportunity for intensive review. It seems to me the hon. member who moved the amendment wrote it out before he had read the bill.
The whole area of estate taxes is one of the most complicated in tax law. It touches on the most personal plans of thousands of people. Some larger estates will be worse off under this measure. I was

speechtext:
In rising to join in this debate, I do so as a member from a province which is presented with a particular problem in this field. My province has a peculiar relationship with this estate tax issue inasmuch as it has declined to profit by this field of


taxation and today rebates to its citizens the provincial share of federal taxes raised in such a way.
As the minister himself has pointed out, 75 per cent of the tax revenue raised by federal estate tax goes back to the provinces. In the province of Alberta, the amount raised by federal tax collectors in this connection is rebated to the individuals concerned. This sounds like a neat, straightforward operation at the end of which the taxpayer is fully recompensed, having suffered no financial loss. Unfortunately, this is not quite the case.
Although the federal tax collectors know that the money will eventually be paid right back to the beneficiaries of the estate, the federal tax collectors still insist on collecting the money, taking it into the federal coffers, and paying a lump sum back to the provinces which must then be rebated by the province to the individuals concerned. Apart from the cost and effort involved in this process, there are two serious drawbacks attached to it. First, those responsible for the collection of federal estate tax insist on prompt and full payment of the tax even though they realize it will eventually be rebated. Second, and this is much more serious, the sum rebated can be viewed as income by the federal government and taxed as such, as pointed out by the hon. member for Edmonton West (Mr. Lambert) in his speech yesterday.
I cannot believe that the minister would have gone to all this trouble, and courted the public abuse he has received in respect of this measure, simply for the sake of the revenue which the estate tax will produce. On his own admission this revenue, according to the estimates he has, will amount only to some $30 million.
Perhaps the answer lies in the income tax revenues which he expects will flow from taxable provincial rebates, particularly in view of the fact that several other provinces have indicated they will follow Alberta's lead in rebating this tax. Whatever his reasons for perpetrating this tax horror on Canadians, the minister has so far shown no public awareness of what the impact will be. He has scrambled a few figures around and made a few more confusing statements, but the main body of his tax measure remains untouched. As it now stands, this tax proposal is a lethal weapon pointed directly at the family farm and the small businesses across Canada. If it becomes law, it will wipe out a large segment of our national, social and economic life within one generation. The minister has made
February 6, 1969	COMMONS
light of this claim and says everyone will be much better off than before. He seems to think that by raising the tax floor from $20,000 to $50,000 people will believe small businesses and family farms will be made safe. If he really believes that, which I doubt, then he is sadly out of touch with the facts of Canada's economic life.
[DOT] (9:30 p.m.)
After all, the revisions announced by the minister on January 30 do not change the exemptions one iota. All he has done has been to say that no estate under $50,000 will be taxed. The $75,000 estate will still be gouged as heavily under the revised proposal as under the original. Thanks to the reckless spending habits of his colleagues of this and previous Liberal governments, inflation and rising costs have made $20,000 look like $50,000 and $50,000 look like $100,000.
Let us take the example of farm units in the province of Alberta. The latest reliable figures are those available in the 1966 agricultural census, and we should remember what has happened to prices and costs since then. I read in the newspaper last night that real estate prices in Ottawa have risen 13 per cent in the past year. If that is true of real estate in this city, just think what has happened to the capital value of farm units since 1966. In that year there were 69,411 farms in Alberta. Of these, only 519 were run by managers. The others were all owner or tenant, or owner-tenant operated. In other words, they were farms that could be designated as family or privately operated farms, not run by syndicates or large corporations.
As of 1966 there were some 30,000 farms in Alberta capitalized at more than $50,000, and another 20,000 or so just under that figure. The latter have probably graduated to the $50,000 figure by now after three years of spiralling costs and inflation. Perhaps these figures, Mr. Speaker, will give the minister some idea of the dimensions of the problem his new estate tax has created for Canadians.
The Saskatchewan Association of Rural Municipalities sent the minister a letter some time ago about his new tax. They drew attention to the menace it posed to farming in particular. The letter reads in part:
Because of high land values and large land holdings which successful farming operations require, farm estates attract large estate taxes but have no liquid assets readily available to pay them. We cannot see how our national wellbeing would be served by the breaking up of production units to pay estate taxes.

Nor do I, Mr. Speaker. The proposed tax system, the letter states:
-will expose the farm estate to taxes which could compel the farm to be broken up and sold.
It is true that the minister has now made an allowance for payment of estate taxes on an instalment basis. This is hardly a measure of relief. It is very like the hangman telling the condemned man that instead of breaking his neck quickly with one short, sharp drop he will be merciful and let him strangle to death slowly.
No, Mr. Speaker, however one looks at this tax it is an iniquitous and unnecessary measure. Personally, I believe in abolishing all taxation of estates. I am unalterably opposed to any action that tends to discourage individual initiative and business enterprise, and even more to any measure that destroys accumulations of private capital. If we pursue such a blind policy as the discouragement of individual business enterprise and the destruction of private capital, the nation is doomed to slow economic death. History is full of examples of what happens to a state that follows this course.
Canada remains ravenously hungry for capital. It is among our largest imports. One of our most pressing needs for the realization of our potential as a people and as a nation, is capital. The last thing we should be doing is taxing our own sources of capital out of existence. One of the most interesting documents on this subject is the report of the Economic Council of Ontario. Last fall the Council finished an exhaustive study of the question for that government. The report notes:
While allegedly aimed at the "redistribution of wealth", these taxes (death duties and estate taxes) are to a very significant degree extracted from individuals who by today's standards cannot be considered wealthy.
And then later on:
One may question whether a $70,000 farm represents an "undue concentration of wealth" when carried to this degree ... (and whether to tax it) ... is economically sound policy.
In its introduction to the chapter on transfer taxes, the description used by the council to cover all estate and similar taxes, the report states:
Though the percentage of revenue from transfer taxes received by the Canadian governments is exceeded among the nations of the western world only by the governments of the United States and United Kingdom, the relative maturity of the economies of these two prominent countries, when
February 6, 1969

Income Tax Act and Estate Tax Act
compared to that of Canada, raises a question as to the merit of thus dissipating and discouraging private accumulations of investment capital.
The answer may well be that most Canadians are unaware that transfer taxes are, in fact taxes levied on investment capital.. . and that Canada ranks above all other nations in the share of taxes raised from all forms of capital investment.
There is irony indeed that Canada, which needs capital almost more than any other western nation, is the most assiduous in destroying the incentive for accumulating such capital and, when such accumulation is made, taxing it out of existence. I am absolutely opposed to this legislation, Mr. Speaker, in theory as well as fact. I believe that instead of considering ways of increasing the tax burden on private capital we should be considering measures to free it entirely from its government-imposed shackles.

subtopic: INCOME TAX ACT AND ESTATE TAX ACT
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, there is no doubt in my mind that the government's proposals for estate taxes have caused a great deal of concern, particularly among rural people. In common, I suppose, with many hon. members I received many letters, indeed hundreds of letters, concerning this subject. Along with the hon. member for York North (Mr. Danson), I have conducted conversations, discussions and meetings with various farm organizations. I found that as we explained to the farm organizations the facts of the matter, a great deal of their concern evaporated. There is a great deal of misunderstanding and misrepresentation,-no doubt accidentally,-in the press in relation to the estate tax, and I think this is very unfortunate. I think this is very unfortunate because the Minister of Finance (Mr. Benson), who should be receiving credit for a progressive piece of legislation, is receiving a few brickbats.
The fact of the matter is that in introducing the five year period to pay, a great progressive step has been taken. The fact of the matter is that in enabling wives to inherit tax free, and receive gifts tax free, a great progressive step has been taken. We have heard a great deal of talk to the effect that the family farm is going to be hit and will probably disappear. The facts are that most family estates are going to be much better off under the new legislation than they were under the old provisions.
I was frankly amazed at the argument presented by the Leader of the Opposition (Mr. Stanfield) in relation to this measure. It is a complex problem. He had a very simple

solution-throw the thing out. Why? Well, there has been a lot of confusion, a lot of misunderstanding. What does that prove? That proves it was really a half-baked idea. Really, I do not think that proves it was a half-baked idea.
[DOT] (9:40 p.m.)
If the government were unprepared to listen to reason he would be the first to complain that they were rigid, that they were stonewalling or that they were arrogant. When the Minister of Finance is prepared to accept reasonable suggestions from people on whatever side of the house he says, "Ah, that proves it was a half-baked idea". He says, "Let us talk straight; let us not have any confusion". Well, let us not have any confusion. Let us talk straight about where he stands on this issue. He says "Throw it out". What does he want to throw out? Does he want to throw out the five year payment principle? Does he want to throw out the fact that wives will receive tax-free inheritances? Does he want to throw out the fact that wives will be able to receive gifts tax free? Does he want to throw out the fact that the gift tax exemption has been effectively nearly doubled? I ask what is it that the hon. Leader of the Opposition (Mr. Stanfield) wants to throw out.
When we get to the hon. member for Crowfoot (Mr. Horner) then the confusion becomes compounded. What does he say? He said that the Minister of Finance says the burden is not too great. Then, this member says "But let us talk to the farm leaders". Let us do more than talk to the farm leaders; let us have a look at the facts. The fact is that the new proposals do not, on an over-all view, reduce exemptions on estates. What they do is provide advantages to estates involving families with children in comparison to those involving families without children. That is because there is a new exemption. Perhaps the Leader of the Opposition wants that thrown out too. There is a new exemption of $10,000 for each child no matter what his age is. It is true that the basic exemption has been lowered from $40,000 to $20,000, but the total exemptions will slide upwards depending on the number of children in the family.
We should really keep in mind that these exemptions in many cases apply twice. That is to say, the exemptions will apply at first on the half of the estate going to the children and they will apply again on the half of the estate which is provided to the wife when it
February 8, 1969	COMMONS
passes to the children upon her death. So, in circumstances I have described the exemptions applied to the estate will be at least equal-and where there are children in most cases they will be more-than at the present time, provided the husband divides his estate between his wife and child.
Now, there is a new gift tax exemption. Perhaps that is something the Leader of the Opposition wants to throw out. It is double the previous exemption. It is not an exemption that applies only to children. It can be given to any person. So, in many cases expensive gifts can be made tax free over a period of time. For example, a man can give $2,000 a year to his son tax free. He can also give $2,000 to his daughter-in-law tax free. He can give $4,000 to his wife tax free and she can pass on $2,000 each to the son and to the daughter-in-law tax free. In one year, therefore, $8,000 can be transferred tax free within a family situation.
It may be true that some family farms or businesses will have difficulty paying their estate tax. But they would have even more difficulty paying if the estate tax changes were not put into effect, both because of the extended time given for payment and because an estate, properly arranged, will now generally pay less tax when there are children in the family.
Estates will quite properly be arranged so as to minimize their tax. If the estates are changed, and if we are dealing with a family estate, the tax levied under the new proposals will almost always be less than at the present time. But if people refuse to take advantage of the opportunity offered them, they may pay more tax. It is misleading to suggest that people will not take advantage of the new provisions. It is even more misleading to imply that if they do not choose to take advantage of these provisions they will be forced to pay higher taxes. The fairest thing is to compare the minimum tax they would have to pay under both the old and new legislation if they take the most advantageous way of arranging their estate. On such a comparison, a family estate will now pay less tax.
Let me illustrate my statement with some figures. The hon. member for Crowfoot had some trouble with his figures and the hon. member for Palliser (Mr. Schumacher) does not really understand the situation very well either. Let us look at the least advantageous situation, that in which there is one child. On an $80,000 estate, if the tax is arranged as favourably as possible there will be a tax 29180-3331

Income Tax Act and Estate Tax Act of $1,500 which is $1,100 less than it would be under the most favourable conditions at the present time. If the tax were paid on an instalment basis the instalment payment would be $300 a year for 5 years; and on an estate of $80,000, at 6 per cent, the income on the assets would be $4,800 a year. Let us go to an estate in the amount of $100,000. The tax would be $3,000. That is down $3,200 if the estate is arranged as favourably as possible. The amount paid on an instalment basis would be $600 a year. And at 6 per cent the amount paid on $100,000 would be $6,000 a year.
Then, we might take an estate of $120,000. The tax would be $9,600. This is down $600 in respect of an estate arranged on the most favourable basis at the present time. The tax on the instalment basis would be $1,920 a year for 5 years and with interest at 6 per cent the amount of return on $120,000 would be $7,200. On an estate of $150,000 the tax would be $15,300. That is down $1,500 over the present situation. The tax on an instalment basis would be $3,060 and the annual income on the asset would be $9,000. On an estate of $200,000 the tax on an estate arranged in the most favourable way would be $26,400. That is down $2,200 over what would be paid under the most favourable circumstances at the present time. The tax instalment would be $5,280 and the revenue at 6 per cent interest would be $12,000 a year.
If we start to deal with estates valued at half a million dollars or more there will be more tax paid than at the present time. It may be that the hon. member for Crowfoot is worried about those estates. I would rather worry about the estate valued at under half a million dollars. So long as we are talking of families with at least one child, and an estate valued at less than half a million dollars, under the new arrangement the tax will be less than under the previous arrangement. Those are the facts, and I wish the hon. member for Crowfoot and the hon. member for Palliser would have a look at them.
Someone might ask whether there should be estate or succession duty taxes at the provincial level. It does not make much sense to have them at the provincial level because one province would then have an effective tax advantage over another unrelated to potential economic advantage. Someone might also ask whether we should have a tax at the federal level. One could say that the amount collected, which is approximately $100 million a year, less than one per cent of the federal budget, is not really worth while.

One could also argue on the social side, as I as a Liberal would argue; that is, I do not like a system where a large accumulation of wealth can be passed on from father to son when the person benefiting has not exerted any effort in accumulating the wealth. I would not want to see a situation where enormous sums of money and the power and influence which is attached to them, could be passed on from generation to generation without some regulation.
[DOT] (9:50 p.m.)
I do think there is a special problem, and a special case, in relation to farming and family enterprises. Succession or estate tax duties may fail unfairly on family and farm enterprises because of unliquid assets. There are two approaches one can take to this problem. You can say let us evaluate or assess the farm land for estate tax purposes at farming value, not at real commercial value and, if later that land is converted to other uses, let us go back and charge retroactive taxes on the property on the basis of real commercial value. I can see certain disadvantages to this. It might lead to an uneconomic use of the land, if the land is high priced because it could be better used in another capacity, and thus reduce efficient use of our economic assets.
Also, if you follow such a procedure there might be an encouragement to a large number of gentlemen farmers to push into farming simply to reduce their other profits by operating farms at a loss. They would be encouraged to do so because of taxation. The proper way to look at this tax reform is in the committee of finance later on this spring or summer.
Really the solution to the problem in relation to family farms is to bring in, not a $50,000 exemption which the minister has suggested, but a $100,000 exemption. This should deal with the problem of family farms. A $100,000 exemption would take account of the increase in respect of the value of farm property in the past ten years. It is a fair figure.
This second, and perhaps more fruitful, approach should be looked at by the Finance committee later in the spring when we are considering reform of the whole taxation system. The important thing to recognize at this stage, as long as we are talking about family estates under this new legislation, is that these estates are going to be better off than

they have been in the past. Whatever injustices or inadequacies there have been in respect of estate taxes, they have been diminished by the progressive steps taken by the present Minister of Finance (Mr. Benson). We may not have come all the way down the road, but we have come down two thirds of the way, as a result of the nature of this progressive legislation.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, a few days ago I asked the Minister of Consumer and Corporate Affairs (Mr. Basford) the following question:
Can the minister tell us when the standing joint Senate-Commons committee on price stability, income and employment, will be established?
The minister's answer on that occasion was very vague. I hope tonight he will answer my question in some way other than by saying that before this joint committee can be established the prices and incomes commission must be established. I hope he will not tell me this, because I already know it.
My question is directed to him for the purpose of speeding up the process of establishing both the commission and the committee. I know they are both essential to the process of dealing with prices and income. The minister's white paper on prices and stability, which will be discussed by the committee on Tuesday, was published about December 20 last. I also know that this idea was not new then. Strangely enough, it was exactly two years to the day when the joint Senate-Commons committee on consumer credit and prices published an interim report. One of the recommendations at that time was that a joint committee be established to review consumer affairs and the state of the Canadian economy. This has already been talked about for two years and considerable thought has been given to it.
February 6, 1969
It is my considered opinion that the state of the Canadian economy is worse now than it was two years ago. I have been quite impatient because there are a great many people in this country looking forward with great anticipation to a study being made with respect to inflation, prices and incomes. These factors are very badly in need of attention.
The cost of living increased over 4 per cent last year. Pensions and allowances have increased by 2 per cent, but this increase does not come close to offsetting the four per cent increase in the cost of living. While wages have been increasing their ratio to the increase in the cost of living has been lessening. When talking about different factors in our economy one must consider that the one thing completely out of line is the increase of profits to large companies. I do not have to go back in history to illustrate this. Let must just refer to an item which appeared today in the Globe and Mail. It states in part:
Higher profits are being reported by a wide range of companies in initial 1968 annual reports.
It continues as follows:
Only four of the first 35 companies to report show lower profits for 1968.
The article refers to a number of companies. I shall only refer to one or two. The Algoma Steel Corporation of Sault Ste. Marie had a profit of $1.70 a share compared with $1.22 cents in 1967.

I could go on through these corporations one by one, but I do not intend to do so. I do want to emphasize that when you look at these factors you find that prices have gone up on the one hand and that the incomes of people have not been keeping pace on the other. They are not now in a position to pay for the things they need. The cost of living has gone up higher and faster than incomes, wages and pensions, yet profits have gone way out of line. These are the things that need to be studied.
The function of the joint committee when it is set up will be to deal with and consider the reports of the commission on prices. Let me
Proceedings on Adjournment Motion read you the minister's own words about the function of the standing parliamentary committee on price stability, incomes and employment, as found in the White Paper:
What is envisaged is a joint committee of the Senate and the House of Commons. It would receive the reports of the commission for review and discussion and would make recommendations.
What will be the reports of that commission? The minister went on to say:
While it will be empowered to make recommendations as to government policy, its main function will be to rally a sense of public responsibility leading to voluntary restraint.
The minister emphasizes very definitely that he does not intend to have anything but voluntary restraints. Let me point out to the minister that what we have right now is forced restraints on certain sectors of our population.

We have forced restraint of the most blatant kind, because these people have no means of raising their income. Parliament has turned -a deaf ear and a blind eye on them.

maintopic: TRANSPORT-LEASING OF WATER LOTS ON CANAL SYSTEMS
TRANSPORT-LEASING OF WATER LOTS ON CANAL SYSTEMS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, on January 29 I asked the Minister of Transport (Mr. Hellyer) whether it was still the department's intention to pursue its program with respect to water-lot leasing on the Trent and Rideau Canal Systems. For the past two years the tourist industry on the Trent and Rideau Canal systems has been threatened with additional taxation by way of water-lot leases. Such legislation, if passed, would affect only the commercial operators on these two canal systems. It would not apply to their competitors on other bodies of water such as the Great Lakes, Muskoka, Couchiching, or Simcoe.
In other words, commercial operators on these two systems are being placed at a distinct disadvantage in relation to commercial operators elsewhere. I venture to suggest there will be numerous cases where property ownership will be in serious dispute; cases where it has never been clearly established whether the shoreline involved does in fact belong to the Crown. Much of this shoreline has never been removed from the deeds of the original and present owners. These people are already paying an annual property tax and, because of the present inflated value of waterfront property, their municipal tax assessments are high. Now the department wants to institute a form of double taxation by forcing them to lease property on which they are already paying a high premium.
There are many questions about such legislation which could well lead to complications. First of all, will the property owner pay for a lease on all improved property? Second, if the property is of such size as to allow for the erection of several docks, will the property-owner pay for a lease on the entire waterfront, or for a lease on each dock, and will he have a choice as to whether to lease the entire property or split it into several separate leases around independent docks?
A further difficulty arises. Due to differences between the nature of one waterfront and another, one operator may have to build a dock out 125 feet or more on a shallow beach-type land contour in order to service a boat docking. On the other hand, another operator, perhaps enjoying access to government improved land which, because it is dredged regularly, is close to deep water, may be able to service the same boat with a 20 foot dock. Nevertheless, the operator with the long dock and the shallow beach will
February 6, 1969

have to pay more for his lease because of the length of his dock, something over which he has no control. This constitutes an inequity in taxation.
Has the government considered how little profit may be derived from the water lot leasing when the costs have been deducted for implementation and enforcement of the program, a program which is being carried out against a very small segment of Canada's third largest industry. I would point out, however, that it is the largest industry in the Kawartha Lakes district which I have the honour to represent.
Since figures for 1968 are not yet available, and since, because of Expo, the 1967 figures would tend to give a distorted view, I am going to quote from 1966 statistics which indicate that 40 million tourists visited Canada in that year, 18 million of whom came to Ontario and over two million to the Kawartha Lakes region. More than one billion tourist dollars were brought in, $398 millions to Ontario. And the 1968 figures should be considerably higher.
However, as a profit-making business the tourist industry is only marginal. High operational costs, competition between lodge operators and the competition provided by an ever-increasing number of private and provincial trailer parks, some of which are now offering plush facilities, have combined to narrow the small margin of profit enjoyed by lodge owners. Now, these same people are threatened with yet another monetary demand. Where, and when, is it going to end?
If the department feels that legislation to lease water lots must go through, surely a simpler and more economical method could be found. In closing, I should like to suggest that the Department of Transport make a further review of the entire program before going ahead with this method of water lot leasing.

speakeroldname: Mr. Walter C. Carter (St. John's West):
maintopic: HOUSING-REMOVAL OF TAX ON BUILDING MATERIALS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, yesterday I asked the Minister of Finance (Mr. Benson) a question dealing with the recommendation made by the task force on housing that the 11 per cent sales tax presently being assessed by the federal government on building materials be eliminated. My question was prompted by a statement attributed to the minister responsible for housing in Vancouver, at which time he was alleged to have stated that the Minister of Finance might juggle a few items in the budget so as to eliminate the federal sales tax on building materials.
In reply to my question, the minister stated that no consideration was being given to the recommendation of the task force with regard to the elimination of this tax. His reply indicates to me that there is nothing but confusion in this government. In my opinion, they have injected confusion into national policy. Some time ago we had the Postmaster General (Mr. Keirans) pontificating about NATO. He said that NATO had to go. Not content with reorganizing the Post Office Department, he is now endeavouring to reorganize the world.

speakerposition: N.D.P. House Leader; Whip of the N.D.P.
maintopic: HOUSING-REMOVAL OF TAX ON BUILDING MATERIALS
speechtext: Might be a good idea.

maintopic: HOUSING-REMOVAL OF TAX ON BUILDING MATERIALS
speechtext:
Not by the Postmaster General, if his reorganization of the post office is any indication.
We have a task force headed by one minister which says: "Take off the 11 per cent tax on housing". The Minister of Finance says: "It will stay on". So, obviously there is no unity whatever in this cabinet. Everyone knows that the 11 per cent sales tax must come off.

maintopic: HOUSING-REMOVAL OF TAX ON BUILDING MATERIALS
speechtext: Everyone but the Minister of Finance.

maintopic: HOUSING-REMOVAL OF TAX ON BUILDING MATERIALS
speechtext:
Exactly. In my opinion it is the greatest single contributing factor to inflating the final cost of housing. This 11 per cent tax often means the difference between owning a home and not owning a home.
Since the Minister of Finance is not here I will direct my question to his parliamentary secretary. Was the so-called task force on housing just another step in the personal publicity campaign of the Minister of Transport
February 6, 1969

Proceedings on Adjournment Motion (Mr. Hellyer)? I ask again: Are the recommendations of the minister and his task force to be pushed aside? Why have a task force headed by a minister if we ignore its recommendations? This government is attempting to take credit for doing something about housing when actually the housing crisis has been brought about by the inflation that has been created by this government.
Canadians are being subjected to what is probably the heaviest burden of taxation in the western world as this government, by its artificially induced inflationary policies, siphons away the prosperity that they have earned. The 10 per cent increase in income tax two years ago, followed by the 3 per cent increase one year ago, the 2 per cent increase for social security, not to mention the vicious increase in estate taxes and this ruinous tax on building materials and homes, in my opinion have contributed to destroying the prosperity of our nation. I say to government members that they should get together and remove this tax on homes, thus giving the average Canadian a chance. The attitude of the Minister of Finance represents outright rejection of the recommendations of the task force on housing headed by the Minister of Transport.
What we have here, Mr. Speaker, is one minister publicly repudiating the advice of another. Of course, I would say that this advice was improperly offered. The Minister of Transport had no business heading a task force. Yet, knowing his great love of, and reliance on, public relations one can see how he was dragged into this situation. But now the position is this: his suggestion has been publicly repudiated and rejected by the Minister of Finance.

maintopic: HOUSING-REMOVAL OF TAX ON BUILDING MATERIALS

The Minister of Transport headed a task force on housing at great expense to the Canadian taxpayer. It is his opinion that in order to provide decent housing accommodation for the average Canadian citizen we must eliminate the 11 per cent sales


tax on building materials. If the Minister of Finance and his other cabinet colleagues refuse to go along with that recommendation, the only honourable thing for the Minister of Transport to do is to resign from cabinet.

maintopic: HOUSING-REMOVAL OF TAX ON BUILDING MATERIALS
speechtext: Hear, hear.

maintopic: HOUSING-REMOVAL OF TAX ON BUILDING MATERIALS
speechtext:
I suggest, too, that unless the government follows through on the recommendations of the minister and the task force he headed, he has no other choice.
A recent release by real estate dealers in Ottawa shows that homes in this area have increased about 34 per cent in price since 1965. Liberal governments have been in power since before 1965. In the city I have the honour to represent, St. John's, we have several public housing projects, but some of them are not working out very well. The latest public housing project in St. John's cost the three levels of government, the municipal council, the provincial government and the federal government, over $20,000 per unit to build. I say that if the only way to bring down the price of homes and provide decent accommodation for our average and low income workers is by having the government enter the housing field, then by all means let the government build houses that the average Canadian can live in without social stigma. The houses ought to be built at prices the average Canadian can afford.
Surely, a time when government expenditures are rising higher and higher-they are up nearly 10 per cent in the latest estimates- is no time for anyone to continue gouging our young people in search of a home. May I conclude with a few more words, Mr. Speaker?

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Finance
maintopic: HOUSING-REMOVAL OF TAX ON BUILDING MATERIALS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the hon. member has provided some heat, but I shall attempt to throw at least a little light on the matter. Everyone can, I think, be sympathetic to the idea of lowering taxes where possible. The Minister of Finance (Mr. Benson) has himself indicated that he would like to be able to propose tax reductions. However, he has pointed to the hard fact, Mr. Speaker, that must be faced and that is if important tax reductions were made at the present time the public would either have to pay the same
February 6, 1969	COMMONS
amount of tax in some other way or go without some service or benefit which it has come to expect from the government.
Estimates based on the value of production of building materials and related statistics led to the conclusion that the sales tax on all building materials now yields over $300 million. The revenue from other materials used in the construction of housing-in other words, single family dwellings, apartment buildings and other units-is even more difficult to estimate but is believed to be between $130 million and $140 million. Thus, if the sales tax on all building materials were to be repealed at this time, I am informed that it would have to be replaced by increasing the rate of sales tax by more than 1.5 percentage points, or increasing the revenue from the present personal income tax by about 7 per cent. In other words, some equivalent measure would have to be introduced.

It would, of course, be very difficult to administer an exemption restricted to building materials used only for housing construction. The tax is paid by the manufacturer of materials who does not know whether the bricks, lumber or glass he produces will be used to build a house or a factory. Any exemption, therefore, would probably have to be administered by refunds or by certificates from builders. It might well be better to consider payments to house or apartment builders or home owners of amounts calculated by some formula which would be approximately equal to the sales tax included in the cost of a housing unit.
In general, Mr. Speaker, the recommendations of the task force with respect to the item raised by the hon. member are certainly deserving of serious consideration.
